extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, astronomers, and advanced readers of Newton's Principia (scholars of classical mechanics)
extracted.subtask_description: Geometric constructions and analytic rules (Newtonian) to determine trajectories, velocities, times, and apsidal motion of bodies under given centripetal-force laws; includes constructive procedures for ellipse/hyperbola/parabola cases and approximations for astronomical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative trigonometric correction series for ellipse locus (ACQ + E + G + I ...)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deniq; capiatur angulus ACq æqualis angulo ACQ + E + G + I &c. & ex cosinu ejus Cr & ordinata pr, quæ est ab sinum qr ut Ellipseos axis minor ad axem majorem, habebitur corporis locus correctus p. ... Convergit autem series infinita ACQ + E + G + I quam celerrime, adeo ut vix unquam opus fuerit ultra progredi quam ad terminum secundum E.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An iterative series of small angular corrections (E, G, I, ...) is used to refine the true anomaly/position on an ellipse; take successive angles whose sines are proportional to successive corrections, compute cosines to obtain corrected ordinates; sign changes apply when intermediate angles become negative. The series converges very rapidly so usually terms beyond the second correction are unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous hyperbola method and logarithmic area construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Non dissimili calculo conficitur Problema in Hyperbola. ... Jungatur CP, & ab A & P ad Asymptoton agantur AI, PK Asymptoto alteri parallelæ, & per Tabulam Logarithmorum dabitur Area AIKP, eiq; æqualis area CPA, quæ subducta de triangulo CPS relinquet aream APS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For hyperbolic orbits use a similar analytic construction: extend to asymptotes, draw parallels from A and P, use logarithmic tables to obtain the area AIKP (equal to CPA), subtract the triangle area to get APS. Then apply successive corrections (½APS - ½A etc.) to obtain the perpendicular abscissa SN and hence PQ and the refined locus Q; repeated computation improves accuracy indefinitely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astronomical practical approximation (angles Y, Z, and equations V,X)
rubrics_metrics.description: Existentibus AO, OB, OD semiaxibus Ellipseos, & L ipsius latere recto, quære tum angulum Y, cujus Tangens sit ad Radium ut est semiaxium differentia AO - OD ad eorum summam AO + OD; tum angulum Z, cujus tangens sit ad Radium ut rectangulum sub umbilicorum distantia SH & semiaxium differentia AO - OD ad triplum rectangulum sub OQ semiaxe minore & AO - ¼L differentia inter semiaxem majorem & quartam partem lateris recti. ... Sume angulum T proportionalem tempori quo arcus BP descriptus est, seu motui medio (ut loquuntur) æqualem; & angulum V (primam medii motus æquationem) ad angulum Y (æquationem maximam primam) ut est sinus anguli T duplicati ad radium; atq; angulum X (æquationem secundam) ad angulum Z (æquationem maximam secundam) ut est sinus versus anguli T duplicati ad radium duplicatum, vel ... ut est quadratum sinus anguli T ad quadratum Radii. ... Invento autem angulo motus medii æquati BHP, angulus veri motus HSP & distantia SP in promptu sunt per methodum notissimam Dris. Sethi Wardi Episcopi Salisburiensis mihi plurimum colendi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practical astronomical algorithm: compute corrective angles Y and Z from ellipse semiaxes and geometry, then compute small equation angles V and X proportional to sines (or squared sines) of double mean motion angle T; combine to form the corrected mean-equalized motion (BHP) or its sum/difference depending on the size of T; locate intersection HP with the ellipse to get point P. Only the first few small correction terms (V and X) need be computed in arcseconds for sufficient accuracy; known methods (Dr. Seth Ward referenced) give conversion to true anomaly and distance SP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXII: Spaces for straight descent under inverse-square centripetal force
rubrics_metrics.description: Posito quod vis centripeta sit reciproce proportionalis quadrato distantiæ locorum a centro, spatia definire quæ corpus recta cadendo datis temporibus describit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the conic section generated by allowing the orbit of a body moving under the given force (ellipse, hyperbola, parabola); relate areas (for example ASD or BDEB) to elapsed time. By decreasing the transverse semi-latus (latus rectum) to zero, the conic perimeter coincides with the straight line, yielding the space described in given time. Cases: if the section is an ellipse, use semicircle area relations; if hyperbola, use limiting process to get rectilinear descent; if parabola, form parabolic segments proportional to time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXIII (Theor. IX): Relation of velocities for inverse-square force
rubrics_metrics.description: Positis jam inventis, dico quod corporis cadentis velocitas in loco quovis C est ad velocitatem corporis centro B intervallo BC circulum describentis, in dimidiata ratione quam CA, distantia corporis a Circuli vel Hyperbolæ vertice ulteriore A, habet ad figuræ semidiametrum principalem ½AB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By geometric limiting of conic sections and tangents, express the falling body's velocity at C in terms of corresponding circular motion velocity about B. The ratio reduces (in the limit) to one involving AC and AO (half the principal semidiameter), giving a rule to compute linear velocities from geometric proportions of the associated conic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXIV (Theor. X): Parabolic special-case velocity equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Si figura BED Parabola est, dico quod corporis cadentis velocitas in loco quovis C æqualis est velocitati qua corpus centro B dimidio intervalli sui BC circulum uniformiter describere potest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the parabolic case the falling body's velocity at any point equals the uniform circular velocity corresponding to half the interval BC; deduced as the limiting case when conic transverse width tends to zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXV (Theor. XI): Area equivalence with a uniformly gyrating body
rubrics_metrics.description: Iisdem positis, dico quod area figuræ DES, radio indefinito SD descripta, æqualis sit areæ quam corpus, radio dimidium lateris recti figuræ DES æquante, circa centrum S uniformiter gyrando, eodem tempore describere potest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For conic/rectilinear cases, equate the area generated by the falling body to the area a uniformly rotating body would describe when given an effective radius equal to half the latus rectum; geometric construction with infinitesimal elements shows the equality of corresponding elemental areas and hence of total areas when integrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXVI (Prob. XXV): Constructing descent times from semicircles
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporis de loco dato A cadentis determinare tempora descensus. Super diametro AS (distantia corporis a centro sub initio) describe semicirculum ADS, ut & huic æqualem semicirculum OKH circa centrum S. ... Patet per Theor. XI, quod corpus cadendo describet spatium AC eodem tempore quo corpus aliud uniformiter circa centrum S gyrando, describere potest arcum OK.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To find the time of descent from a given point, construct a semicircle on AS and an equal semicircle about S; erect the ordinate CD at the chosen point C and find the corresponding section OSK equal to area ASD; by Theorem XI the arc OK gives the equal time for a uniformly rotating body, so the descent time corresponds to that arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXVII (Prob. XXVI): Times for ascent/descent with given initial velocity
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporis de loco dato sursum vel deorsum projecti definire tempora ascensus vel descensus. Exeat corpus de loco dato G secundum lineam ASG cum velocitate quacunq;. In duplicata ratione hujus velocitatis ad uniformem in circulo velocitatem ... cape CA ad ½AS. ... Patet hoc per Theorema X. Sin ratio illa minor vel major est quam 2 ad 1, priore casu Circulus, posteriore Hyperbola rectangula ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given an initial speed, compare it (squared) to the uniform circular speed to determine whether the trajectory corresponds to a circle, parabola, or hyperbola; construct appropriate concentric circles or conics and erect ordinates to find heights and use equal-area/sectors to equate times of ascent/descent to arcs described by equivalent uniform circular motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXVIII (Theor. XII): Force proportional to distance — arcs and sines proportionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Posito quod vis centripeta proportionalis sit altitudini seu distantiæ locorum a centro, dico quod cadentium tempora, velocitates & spatia descripta sunt arcubus arcuumq; sinibus versis & sinibus rectis respective proportionales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the centripetal force is proportional to distance (harmonic force), then times correspond to arcs, velocities to versed sines (or sine of arc), and spaces to sines themselves; use a circle/quadrant construction (AE, CD as sine of arc AD) to map times, spaces and velocities to trigonometric measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXIX (Prob. XXVII): From any centripetal law and quadratures derive rectilinear velocities and times
rubrics_metrics.description: Posita cujuscunq; generis vi centripeta, & concessis figurarum curvilinearum quadraturis, requiritur corporis recta ascendentis vel descendentis tum velocitas in locis singulis, tum tempus quo corpus ad locum quemvis perveniet: Et contra.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given a centripetal force law and the ability to quadrate (compute areas under) certain curves, one can derive the velocity at each location (velocity ∝ square-root of area-related quantity) and the time to traverse to any location (time ∝ area under a related curve). Conversely, given velocities/times one may construct the necessary curve quadratures. The proof uses infinitesimal area elements and the relation between increments of velocity and generated areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries to Prop. XXXIX: computing loci, velocities, and times via areas/rectangles
rubrics_metrics.description: In EG capiatur EM lateri quadrato areæ ABGE reciproce proportionalis, & sit ALM linea curva quam punctum M perpetuo tangit, & erit tempus quo corpus cadendo describit lineam AE ut area curvilinea ALME. ... Corol. 1., Corol. 2., Corol. 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical corollaries: construct an ordinate EM inversely proportional to the square of the latus related to an area to obtain a curve whose tangent the particle follows; time to descend a given segment equals the area under the constructed curve. For known comparative forces one can construct rectangles and subtractions (PDRQ etc.) to locate loci P giving required motion equivalences; explicit algebraic relations (involving square roots of area differences) give velocities and reciprocals for times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XL (Theor. XIII): Equal-altitude equal-velocity equivalence between rectilinear and curved motions
rubrics_metrics.description: Si corpus, cogente vi quacunq; centripeta, moveatur utcunq;, & corpus aliud recta ascendat vel descendat, sintq; eorum velocitates in aliquo æqualium altitudinum casu æquales, velocitates eorum in omnibus æqualibus altitudinibus erunt æquales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two bodies (one in arbitrary curve, one in rectilinear motion) have equal velocities at one common altitude under the same centripetal force law, then their velocities are equal at all equal altitudes. The argument uses concentric circles and decomposition of forces into transverse and radial components and the equality of generating accelerations in infinitesimal passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries to Prop. XL: applications (pendulum, projection equivalences, velocity formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corol. 1. Hinc si corpus vel funipendulum oscilletur, vel impedimento quovis politissimo & perfecte lubrico cogatur in linea curva moveri, & corpus aliud recta ascendat vel descendat, sintq; velocitates eorum in eadem quacunq; altitudine æquales: erunt velocitates eorum in aliis quibuscunq; æqualibus altitudinibus æquales. Corol. 2. Hinc etiam si quantitas P sit maxima a centro distantia ... velocitas corporis in omni altitudine A erit ut [sqrt]{nP^n - nA^n}, atq; adeo datur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the proposition to equate motions of pendula or ideally lubricated constrained bodies with rectilinear descent; gives explicit velocity formula when centripetal force varies as A^{n-1} (power-law) producing v ∝ sqrt(nP^n - nA^n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XLI (Prob. XXVIII): Given centripetal law, construct the trajectory and determine motion times
rubrics_metrics.description: Posita cujuscunq; generis vi centripeta & concessis figurarum curvilinearum quadraturis, requiruntur tum Trajectoriæ in quibus corpora movebuntur, tum tempora motuum in Trajectoriis inventis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: draw an auxiliary circle VXY about the center, let it intersect secondary circles ID, KE and recta CNIX; define a small reference altitude A so that IK/KN = sqrt(ABFD)/Z, construct appropriate infinitesimal rectangles proportional to given quantities, and from equalities of generated elemental areas obtain the sector/area relations (VDba, VDdc) that determine altitude CI (locus I) at the given time. This yields a constructive method: given time, compute the corresponding area/sector and hence the point on the trajectory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries to Prop. XLI (finding apsides and intersection angles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corol. 1. Hinc maximæ minimæq; corporum altitudines, id est Apsides Trajectoriarum expedite inveniri possunt. ... Corol. 2. Sed & angulus KIN ... ex data corporis altitudine CI expedite invenitur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the construction one can rapidly locate apsides (max/min altitudes) where IC cut the trajectory orthogonally (IK = KN) corresponding to ABFD = ZZ; and compute intersection angles by taking sines proportional to Z relative to the area-latus square ABFD.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XLII (Prob. XXIX): Given force law and initial position/velocity, determine later motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Data lege vis centripetæ, requiritur motus corporis de loco dato data cum velocitate secundum datam rectam egressi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given initial line of motion and an initial velocity (comparable to what would be obtained by falling a certain altitude), construct auxiliary circles, build families of curves (ALMm, BFGg, abzv, dcxw) by the procedure of Prob. XXVIII and the associated corollary; from the given rectangle PDRQ and the known centripetal law, one obtains the curve family and hence, for any time, the altitude and area sector to determine the position on the trajectory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XLIII (Prob. XXX): Make a body move in a chosen trajectory in a revolving frame as in the immobile frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Efficiendum est ut corpus in Trajectoria quacunq; circa centrum virium revolvente perinde moveri possit, atq; corpus aliud in eadem Trajectoria quiescente.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct for the revolving frame a point p whose angular relation VCp:VCP matches a given ratio so that the area described by Cp is to area VCP as their respective angular speeds; choose the centripetal force of appropriate magnitude so that the body in the revolving frame describes the same relative arc per time as the body in the immobile frame. Use area-angular speed proportionality to deduce the required centripetal force (solve the problem by proportion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XLIV (Theor. XIV): Difference of forces between immobile and revolving orbit (inverse-cube altitude law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentia virium, quibus corpus in Orbe quiescente, & corpus aliud in eodem Orbe revolvente æqualiter moveri possunt, est in triplicata ratione communis altitudinis inverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two similar equal orbits (one immobile, one rotating) are considered, the difference of the centripetal forces required to produce equal motions in the same trajectory is proportional to the inverse cube of the common altitude (distance from center). Corollaries give explicit algebraic forms for forces in ellipses and circles (e.g., add {RG^2 - RF^2}/A^3 to F^2/A^2 term) and show how to derive forces at any altitude A from values at a reference altitude CV.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XLV (Prob. XXXI): Apsidal motion of nearly circular orbits via series expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: Orbium qui sunt Circulis maxime finitimi requiruntur motus Apsidum. Problema solvitur Arithmetice faciendo ut orbis, quem corpus in Ellipsi mobili, ... accedat ad formam orbis cujus Apsides requiruntur, & quærendo Apsides orbis quem corpus illud in plano immobili describit. ... Exempl. 1. Ponamus vim centripetam uniformem esse, adeoq; ut A cub. ÷ A cub. ... Jam cum Orbis ponatur circulo quam maxime finitimus, coeat orbis cum circulo; & ob factas R, T æquales, atq; X in infinitum diminutam, rationes ultimæ erunt RGq. ad T cub. ut -Fq. ad -3Tq. seu Gq. ad Tq.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To compute apsidal precession for orbits nearly circular, expand the centripetal-force expression in powers (substitute A = T - X etc.), collect like terms in the numerator and denominator to obtain limiting ratios as the orbit tends to a circle. Use these algebraic expansions to derive the rate of apsidal advance for a given force law; worked examples (e.g., uniform centripetal force) demonstrate the extraction of limiting ratios.
